newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Denktash talks tough ahead of Cyprus talks.
newsitem.headline: Denktash talks tough ahead of Cyprus talks.

text.p: Prospects for U.N.-brokered talks in Switzerland aimed at reuniting Cyprus looked grim on Sunday as Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash arrived in Geneva saying he is not prepared to give in to pressure for compromise.
Denktash spoke negatively on prospects for a deal on the eve of five days of talks with Cyprus president Glafcos Clerides, saying the Turkish Cypriot position had been ignored.

In an interview with Reuters, he spelt out his tough stance, accusing the international community of not listening to his side and the European Union of getting in the way of a deal at the talks starting on Monday at Glion near the city of Montreux.
"We're entering a crucial negotiating process," he said. "We have been defending political equality, that sovereignty is not Greek Cypriot sovereignty but bi-communal sovereignty."

"Therefore, we have basic legal and political rights which have to be accepted. Mr Clerides is on the record saying that he is not going to discuss sovereignty with us. We are not going to discuss sovereignty with him because we are sovereign."
The talks aimed at reuniting the divided island under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation follow a first round last month in Troutbeck, New York.
Stakes have since been raised with the EU announcing plans for entry talks for Cyprus early next year and Turkey saying it will move towards partial integration with the north.
The insistence of Turkish Cypriots -- who make up 18 percent of the island's population but control 37 percent of the land -- on sovereign equality is one of the key sticking points.
Positions of both sides contain elements anathema to the other, such as the Greek Cypriot wish for freedom of settlement.

Greek and Turkish Cypriots have been estranged since 1963, three years after independence from Britain, when a government representing both communities broke apart amid violence that led to the dispatch of a U.N. peacekeeping force still in Cyprus.
They have been forcibly separated since 1974 when Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in response to a coup in the capital Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.
The Turkish Cypriot state proclaimed in 1983 with Denktash as president is recognised only by Ankara.
On the table in Glion is a U.N.-drafted document calling on the two communities to commit themselves to a sustained process of open-ended, direct negotiations.
Diplomats close to the talks said the two sides remained far apart with little progress expected at the meeting -- described by one source as "keeping up the appearances".
Denktash accused the EU of destroying chances for a settlement by announcing plans for entry talks for Cyprus and reiterated that he would pull out of the talks if this happened.

"We want the EU to understand that by interfering with the affairs of Cyprus at a very crucial stage, by giving a green light to one of the parties to represent the whole island and to become a member, it destroyed chances of a settlement," he said.
Denktash said he was prepared for the talks to break down rather than compromise on sovereignty and EU membership talks.
"If the EU talks start, the intercommunal talks will stop and that will be the end of the matter," he said.

"If the EU accession talks begin and we stop intercommunal talks, as we must, naturally we'll take the same steps vis-a-vis Turkey as the Greek Cypriot side will take vis-a-vis the EU. We have an alternative. We don't depend on a future solution."

Denktash said the New York talks came close to collapse because of the EU position: "At Troutbeck, I should have walked out but I didn't. They (Greek Cypriots) are now on a new track which is not taking us into a negotiated settlement and is leading us to counter-action."
"We are not going to be colonised by the Greek Cypriots. Under the law, they are not our government, under the agreements they are not, in fact they are not and they cannot be."
